content: In February 1999, the National Cancer Institute (USA) issued an alert recommending that concomitant chemoradiotherapy should be considered for all patients with cervical cancer. This recommendation was based on evidence from five randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The purpose of this review was to analyze all known RCTs that compared concomitant chemotherapy and radiation therapy with radiation therapy alone for the treatment of locally advanced cervical cancer. To conduct this review, electronic databases, trial registries, and reference lists of published trial reports and review articles were searched. The review included RCTs that compared concomitant chemoradiation with radiotherapy in the experimental arm. Trials that allowed additional adjuvant chemotherapy or hydroxyurea were included, but those using radiosensitizers or radioprotectors in the experimental arm were excluded. Two authors independently reviewed the trials for inclusion and extracted data. For outcomes such as survival and progression-free survival, hazard ratios (HRs) were extracted or estimated from trial reports when possible. Many reports only provided overall rates of local and distant recurrence, so odds ratios (ORs) were calculated for recurrence rates, which do not account for time to recurrence or censoring. Acute toxicity was not consistently reported, but when data were available, ORs were calculated for the main types and severities of acute toxicity. The HRs and ORs from individual trials were combined using a fixed-effect model. Late toxicity was rarely described in sufficient detail, so it was only reviewed qualitatively. The original review included 19 trials (17 published and 2 unpublished) with a total of 4,580 patients. This updated review includes 24 trials (21 published and 3 unpublished) with 4,921 patients. However, due to patient exclusions and differential reporting, only 61% to 75% of the patients were available for analysis. The findings strongly suggest that concomitant chemoradiation improves both overall survival and progression-free survival, with absolute benefits of 10% and 13%, respectively. However, there was statistical heterogeneity in these outcomes. The benefit appeared to be greater in trials that included a high proportion of patients with stage I and II disease. Concomitant chemoradiation also significantly reduced local recurrence and showed a potential benefit in reducing distant recurrence. However, acute hematological and gastrointestinal toxicities were significantly higher in the chemoradiation group. The long-term side effects of treatment were not well reported, so the impact of chemoradiation on late toxicity remains unclear. Treatment-related deaths were rare. In conclusion, concomitant chemoradiation appears to improve overall survival and progression-free survival in patients with locally advanced cervical cancer. It also reduces local and distant recurrence, suggesting that concomitant chemotherapy may enhance radiosensitization and provide systemic cytotoxic effects. While acute toxicity is increased, the long-term side effects of this treatment approach are still not well understood.
